section.heading: 3.6. Derivatives of Logarithmic and Inverse Trigonometric Functions
section.paragraph: In this section we use implicit differentiation to find derivatives of logarithmic functions and of inverse trigonometric functions.
section.heading: Derivatives of Logarithmic Functions
section.paragraph: In Appendix F we prove that if $$f$$ is a one-to-one differentiable function, then its inverse function $$f^{- 1}$$ is also differentiable, except where its tangents are vertical. This is plausible because, geometrically, we can think of a differentiable function as one whose graph has no corner or cusp. We obtain the graph of $$f^{- 1}$$ by reflecting the graph of $$f$$ about the line $$y = x$$ , so the graph of $$f^{- 1}$$ has no corner or cusp either. (Note that if $$f$$ has a horizontal tangent at a point, then $$f^{- 1}$$ has a vertical tangent at the corresponding reflected point and so $$f^{- 1}$$ is not differentiable there.)

Because the logarithmic function $$y = \log_{b}x$$ is the inverse of the exponential function $$y = b^{x}$$ , which we know is differentiable from Section 3.1, it follows that the logarithmic function is also differentiable. We now state and prove the formula for the derivative of a logarithmic function.
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}{({\log_{b}x})} = \frac{1}{x\ln b}$$

section.paragraph: If we put $$b = e$$ in Formula 1, then the factor $$\ln b$$ on the right side becomes $$\ln e = 1$$ and we get the formula for the derivative of the natural logarithmic function $$\log_{e}x = \ln x$$ :
$$\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( {\ln x} \right) = \frac{1}{x}$$

By comparing Formulas 1 and 2, we see one of the main reasons that natural logarithms (logarithms with base $$e$$ ) are used in calculus: The differentiation formula is simplest when $$b = e$$ because $$\ln e = 1$$ .

Recall that the general version of the Power Rule states that if $$n$$ is any real number and $$f(x) = x^{n}$$ , then $$f^{\prime}(x) = nx^{n - 1}$$ .

section.heading: The Number e as a Limit
section.paragraph: We have shown that if $$f(x) = \ln x$$ , then $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1 \slash x$$ . Thus $$f^{\prime}(1) = 1$$ . We now use this fact to express the number $$e$$ as a limit.
From the definition of a derivative as a limit, we have

$$\begin{array}{lll} {{f^{\prime}(1)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {1 + h} \right) - f(1)}{h}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {1 + x} \right) - f(1)}{x}}} & & \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(1)} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\ln\left( {1 + x} \right) - \ln 1}{x}} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{x}\ln\left( {1 + x} \right)}} & & \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(1)} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\ln\left( {1 + x} \right)^{1 \slash x}}} & & \end{array}$$
Because $$f^{\prime}(1) = 1$$ , we have
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\ln\left( {1 + x} \right)^{1 \slash x} = 1$$
Then, by Theorem 2.5.8 and the continuity of the exponential function, we have
$$e = e^{1} = e^{\lim_{x\rightarrow 0}\ln{({1 + x})}^{1 \slash x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}e^{\ln{({1 + x})}^{1 \slash x}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}{({1 + x})}^{1 \slash x}$$
$$e = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}(1 + x)^{1 \slash x}$$

section.heading: Derivatives of Inverse Trigonometric Functions
section.paragraph: The inverse trigonometric functions were reviewed in Section 1.5. We discussed their continuity in Section 2.5 and their asymptotes in Section 2.6. Here we use implicit differentiation to find their derivatives. At the beginning of this section we observed that if $$f$$ is a one-to-one differentiable function, then its inverse function $$f^{- 1}$$ is also differentiable (except where its tangents are vertical). Because the trigonometric functions—with the restricted domains that we used to define their inverses—are one-to-one and differentiable, it follows that the inverse trigonometric functions are also differentiable.

and
$$- \frac{\pi}{2} \leqslant y \leqslant \frac{\pi}{2}$$
Differentiating $$\sin y = x$$ implicitly with respect to $$x$$ , we obtain
$$\cos y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = 1$$
or
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{1}{\cos y}$$
Now $$\cos y \geqslant 0$$ , since $$- \pi \slash 2 \leqslant y \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$ , so
$$\cos y = \sqrt{1 - \sin^{2}y} = \sqrt{1 - x^{2}} \left( \cos^{2}y + \sin^{2}y = 1 \right)$$
Therefore
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{1}{\cos y} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}$$

The formula for the derivative of the arctangent function is derived in a similar way. If $$y = \tan^{- 1}x$$ , then $$\tan y = x$$ . Differentiating $$\tan y = x$$ implicitly with respect to $$x$$ , we have
$$\begin{array}{rll} {\sec^{2}y\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}}} & = & 1 \\ \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} & = & {\frac{1}{\sec^{2}y} = \frac{1}{1 + \tan^{2}y} = \frac{1}{1 + x^{2}}} \end{array}$$

Figure 5 shows the graph of $$f(x) = \tan^{- 1}x$$ and its derivative $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1 \slash {({1 + x^{2}})}$$ . Notice that $$f$$ is increasing and $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is always positive. The fact that $$\left. \tan^{- 1}x\rightarrow \pm \pi \slash 2 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ is reflected in the fact that $$\left. f^{\prime}(x)\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ as $$\left. x\rightarrow \pm \infty \right.$$ .
